Transistors have always been analog devices, not limited to just two states. The reason digital electronics work so well is that two states can easily be propagated quickly, because the transistor can be operating as a very high gain (high slew rate) amplifier that saturates to one power rail. With multiple states the gain must be much more carefully controlled.

Another superiority of two-state logic is noise immunity; the more states the less distance between valid states. The issue comes up with modern MLC flash chips which store more than one bit per transistor as varying levels of charge. Here it's acceptable because it allows many times the density, and the memory interface can implement error correction on blocks of data.

And finally efficiency-wise, a transistor being fully on or fully off draws nearly no current, but maintaining something between acts as a resistance so dissipates power continuously.
